newsitem.title: INDIA: India IOC denies borrowing limit reached.
newsitem.headline: India IOC denies borrowing limit reached.

text.p: Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) on Wednesday denied a newspaper report that the company had exhausted an enhanced $3.5 billion external commercial borrowing (ECB) limit and said there was no danger of its crude purchases being disrupted.
"It is incorrect that we have reached our ECB limit," an IOC spokesman said.
Asked if IOC, which has a monopoly over crude imports, was close to running out of money to pay for crude imports, he replied; "There is no immediate danger of that."

The Business Standard newspaper reported on Wednesday that IOC had told the government it has exhausted its ECB limit, and it would not be able to raise more loans in international markets as its debt/equity ratio had touched two to one.
The report also said the IOC warned that it could lead to a serious disruption of petroleum supplies.
The IOC spokesman said the government owed IOC around 100 billion rupees ($2.79 billion) from the oil pool account deficit.
IOC imported more than 30 million tonnes of crude in 1996/7 (April-March).

The oil pool deficit represents money owed to Indian oil companies for selling crude and products below market prices in order to support India's complex cross subsidy system for petroleum products known as the administered pricing mechanism.
The United Front coalition government's steering committee will meet on Sunday to discuss raising petroleum product prices in order to whittle down the burgeoning oil pool deficit.

The steering committee has met twice on the subject without reaching a decision, as left parties in the 15-member coalition fought a rearguard action against pressure from Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and the Finance Ministry to raise prices.

At the end of March the oil pool deficit stood at 155 billion rupees, of which time IOC was owed 90 billion, Hindustan Petroleum Corp 18 billion, Oil and Natural Gas Corp 18 billion and Bharat Petroleum Corp 13 billion.

"IOC is keen that the oil pool deficit is bridged as soon as possible, as all the oil companies are, so they can fund their budgets. Otherwise, it will have long term repercussions on infrastructure development, the IOC spokesman said.

He said that while the newspaper's assertation that IOC had hit its ECB limit was wrong, IOC is likely to have told the government that if the oil pool deficit grows unchecked the borrowing limit will be reached in the future.
"There is still scope (within the ECB limit)," he said.
He said there was a risk that the limit would be reached sooner if there was a sudden surge in oil demand or prices.
The long term issue for IOC and the other oil companies was how to pay for major capital investment.
"If borrowing is going to continue for imports only, where will the money come from for infrastructure development.

The Business Standard report said the state-run firm warned the government of the possibility that oil supplies will be disrupted, and domestic refiners will reduce production because of an inability to pay for crude.

"IOC is learnt to have informed the government that the $500 million raised by it recently in Singapore could be the last foreign loan arranged by it under the current difficult oil pool position," the paper said.
"Foreign banks may not risk their capital till the oil pool situation improves," it said.

The IOC spokesman said any government action to whittle down the oil pool deficit would take time to improve the company's cash position, but it would send out an immediate positive signal to investors and bankers.
